notes.steep724: All three are 7:24 tapers (3.5 in per foot, included angle 16.594 deg) with the same gauge diameters; they differ in the flange, the drive slots and the retention knob. ISO 7388-1 (forms A/AD/AF, the DIN 69871 "SK" holder) and ISO 7388-2 (form J, the JIS B 6339 / MAS 403 "BT" holder) are metric; CAT (ASME B5.50, ISO 7388-1 form U) uses an inch thread. Retention knobs (pull studs): ISO 7388-3:2016 (forms AD, AF, UD, UF, JD, JF), ASME B5.50 for CAT and JIS B 6339 for BT. Knob profiles and angles differ between machine builders, so check the machine manual before ordering.
notes.morse: Morse tapers are self-holding (about 1:20, roughly 5/8 in per foot; each size has its own ratio). Gauge diameter = diameter at the gauge line (the large end of the socket). Current standard: ISO 296:1991 (self-holding tapers for tool shanks), with DIN 228-1 the matching German standard. Morse 4 1/2 is rare and the two publishers disagree on it. Included angle = 2 atan(taper per foot / 24).
notes.jacobs: Jacobs tapers hold drill chucks on arbors; they are not Morse tapers and the taper per foot differs between sizes (about 0.59 to 0.98 in per foot). Values as published for the Jacobs Chuck series; the drill chuck tapers of DIN 238 (B-series) are a different, metric family and are not listed here. The JT 6 and JT 33 sizes sit between JT 2 and JT 3 in diameter.
notes.hsk: HSK hollow taper shank with flange face contact. Current standard: ISO 12164-1:2023 (shanks of types A, AB, C, CB and EB); DIN 69893-1 is the original German standard. Size = flange diameter d1 in mm (HSK-A 63 has d1 = 63 mm). HSK holders are clamped from inside by the spindle's clamping mechanism, so there is no pull stud. Only one free publisher found so far for the taper diameters; check the holder maker's drawing.
notes.r8: R8 is a collet and toolholder taper used on knee mills (Bridgeport type), held by a 7/16-20 UNF drawbar. No international standard for R8 was found; dimensions are as published, from one source so far.
notes.jarno: Jarno tapers follow one rule: for taper number N the large end is N/8 in, the small end N/10 in and the length N/2 in, so every size tapers 0.600 in per foot (1:20 on the diameter). Two publishers print the table and it follows the rule in every row; a third prints the rule with No. 8 as its example. One table also prints a longer overall shank length, which is not shown here.
notes.brownsharpe: Brown & Sharpe tapers are self-holding, about 1/2 in per foot (No. 10 is printed as 0.5161). The two publishers print the same small end diameters, but different lengths, and so different large end diameters, for sizes 4, 5, 7, 9, 10 and 11: the same taper made to a longer or shorter plug. Both are shown. Measure the socket before making a shank. The taper per foot column is from one publisher; the other states 0.500 in per foot for the series. Lengths printed as fractions are entered as exact decimals.

trial_steps.t: Take a scrap piece of the same material as the job and chamfer its end.
trial_steps.why: The right blank is best found on scrap of similar material. The chamfer is BenchMate's advice, so the knurl starts on a clean edge.

trial_steps.t: Turn it to the diameter you want to try, measure it and write the diameter down.
trial_steps.why: If you have a calculated blank from one of the other methods, get within 0.001 to 0.002 in (0.03 to 0.05 mm) of it. Hold the blank closely from part to part: 0.0005 in on the blank shows as about 0.001 in on the knurled diameter.

trial_steps.t: Oil the knurls and the work, and set a slow speed.
trial_steps.why: The sources differ on speed. For small manual lathes: about 100 rpm for 1/2 in of soft material (Sherline), 150 to 200 rpm (pjsminilathe). For production knurling GenSwiss gives an upper limit of about 150 sfm (50 m/min), and about 50 sfm (15 m/min) for harder steels and stainless. Start slow.

trial_steps.t: Bring the knurl up until it just touches, add light pressure and turn the spindle by hand about two turns.
trial_steps.why: A light first impression shows whether the knurl tracks before the piece is spoiled.

trial_steps.t: Look at the marks: one clean set of lines, even across the width of the wheel, means it tracks.
trial_steps.why: Tracking is usually settled after one full turn of the part. A second set of lines between the first is double tracking.

trial_steps.t: If it double tracks, first try a firmer first bite. If it still does, change the blank by about 0.005 in (0.13 mm), up or down, and start again at step 2.
trial_steps.why: More infeed usually cures double tracking on bump and cut knurling (GenSwiss). The 0.005 in step is Dorian's for a knurl that double tracks; Sherline gives the same amount, up or down, for a diameter that does not knurl properly.

trial_steps.t: When it tracks, start the spindle and go to full depth in as few turns as you can, with plenty of oil.
trial_steps.why: Bump knurling: 0.001 to 0.004 in per revolution (0.025 to 0.1 mm), finished in 5 to 20 revolutions (GenSwiss). Oil washes the chips out and keeps the knurls from seizing on their pins (Hoffman).

trial_steps.t: Measure the knurled diameter and enter it below to get the growth.
trial_steps.why: Form knurling raises the diameter by an amount that depends on pitch, material and depth; cut knurling barely changes it. The makers' allowance tables are approximate, so the trial piece is the measure.

trial_steps.t: Write down the blank, speed and growth that worked for this knurl and material.
trial_steps.why: BenchMate's advice: the next job with the same knurl and material then starts from a diameter that is known to track.

rules.t: Start in a guide bushing or a pilot hole. Pilot hole: 1 to 2 diameters deep and 0.0005 to 0.0010 in (0.013 to 0.025 mm) larger than the gundrill (Sterling, quoted in Cutting Tool Engineering); 1.5 x D deep (Hartner, to H8; Ingersoll).
Do not run a gundrill at speed outside the hole: it whips. Sterling's table gives the longest unsupported length by diameter; Hartner says to enter the pilot hole at about 200 rev/min and 500 mm/min.

Flow matters more than pressure: the chips leave only if enough coolant reaches the tip. Pressure rises as the drill gets smaller: 200 to 400 psi can be enough on 2 in drills, 1,500 psi and more on very small ones (Drill Masters Eldorado); about 1,000 psi (69 bar) is common on Swiss-type lathes and most gundrilling machines give two to three times that (UNISIG).

Water-soluble coolant: 10 to 12 % (Drill Masters Eldorado; Ingersoll calls 10 to 12 % acceptable and 12 to 15 % preferred, under 8 % not acceptable), 10 to 15 % (ISCAR), at least 10 % oil (Hartner). botek rates deep-hole drilling oil as highly suitable and emulsion as suitable to a limited degree.
Keep the coolant clean and cool: filtered to under 20 um and at 20 to 22 C (ISCAR); 70 to 75 F and not above 130 F (ISCAR, quoted in Cutting Tool Engineering).
Over 30 diameters deep, reduce the feed by 20 % (Sterling). The page does this when a depth is entered.
Straightness to expect: typically 0.001 in per inch of depth (Star SU, quoted in Cutting Tool Engineering).

rules.t: Tighten a collet nut with a torque wrench or a torque block, not by feel.
The most a collet nut should see is 25 % above the recommended torque. More torque means more stress on the holder and can damage it.
Too much torque on a pull stud can deform the small end of the taper, and the holder then runs out in the spindle.
No grease or anti-seize on the pull stud thread; light oil is fine.

Check pull stud torque as part of scheduled maintenance. Replace pull studs at least every three years, and about every year on several shifts, many tool changes or heavy cuts with long or heavy tools.

macro.text: #0 is always empty (null) and cannot be assigned.
#1 to #33 are local variables: a macro call's arguments land here, and they are cleared when the macro or program ends.
Common variables are shared between programs; the ranges depend on the control and builder (see the disagreement note).
#1000 and up are system variables: interface signals, offsets, positions, modal state, alarms and clocks. Numbers depend on the control model, so check its manual.
Arithmetic + - * /. Functions include SIN, COS, TAN (degrees), SQRT, ABS, FIX (round down) and ROUND.
Comparisons EQ, NE, GT, GE, LT, LE. Logic AND, OR.
IF [condition] GOTO n jumps to block Nn when the condition is true. IF [condition] THEN statement runs one statement.
WHILE [condition] DO m ... END m repeats while true; loops can be nested up to 3 deep (DO1 to DO3).
G65 P<program> <arguments> calls a macro once; the macro ends with M99. G66 calls it modally, G67 cancels.
Writing to #3000 raises an operator alarm; #3006 is used for an operator message (sources differ on whether it stops: see disagreements).
Macros are an option: in this document the control needs the macro option enabled (parameter 57 bit 22, ENABLE MACRO). With it off, macro statements are treated as comments.
#1 to #33 are local, cleared at program end; G65 arguments map to them (A #1, B #2, C #3 ... X #24, Z #26).

disagreements.text: The 0i-F lathe manual (B-64604EN-1/01) lists G35 and G36 as circular threading clockwise and counter-clockwise. A third-party A/B/C table (mfgrobots) lists G36 and G37 as automatic tool compensation in X and Z. Both functions exist on Fanuc lathes; which number does which depends on the model and parameters. Check your manual.

disagreements.topic: Selecting G-code system A, B or C
disagreements.text: The maker's lathe manual says the system is chosen with bits 6 (GSB) and 7 (GSC) of parameter 3401. A third-party article says bit 0 of parameter 3401 (0 = A, 1 = B). BenchMate follows the maker's manual.

Tornos says writing #3000 raises an alarm that stops the program and #3006 shows a message without stopping. CNCCookbook says #3000 shows a message (alarm) and #3006 also stops the program. Test on your control before relying on either. cncmacrosimulator.com calls #3006 an operator message and does not say whether it stops. On the older Haas control #3006 stops like M00 (see the Haas list).

CNCCookbook gives #100-#199 (cleared at power-off) and #500-#999 (kept at power-off). Tornos, for its FANUC-controlled machines, gives #150-#199 per channel and #600-#699 shared. Ranges depend on the control model, options and machine builder.
The 2015 mill programming workbook lists G87 (bore, manual retract) and G88 (bore, dwell, manual retract). The current online operator's manual summary table does not list them.
The 2002 Haas lathe card gives tailstock chuck clamp / unclamp; the 2024 Haas Factory Outlet manual gives secondary spindle chuck clamp / unclamp.

Two third-party Okuma lathe lists share the same text. One prints G95 as 'feed per minute (mm/rev)', the other as feed per revolution. The maker's manual describes G94 and G95 as feed per minute and per revolution.

The third-party Okuma lathe lists give M98 / M99 as tailstock spindle thrust low / high, not subprogram call and return. The maker's section 5 text that was readable stops before M98, so this is not confirmed; it is a reminder not to assume Fanuc meanings on an Okuma.
The Haas macro document says #100-#199 and #500-#600 are reserved for Haas (probing, pallet changer) and #600-#699 and #800-#999 are for the user; #600 appears in both ranges as printed.

disagreements.topic: Macro variable number for one tool offset
disagreements.text: Both sources put length wear in the #10000 block, length geometry in the #11000 block, radius wear in the #12000 block and radius geometry in the #13000 block. cncmacrosimulator.com prints the ranges as #10001 to #10400 and so on, which makes offset 200 number #11200. CNCCookbook's example for offset 200 gives #11201 (and #2400 in the older numbering, which fits a block that starts at #2201). The number of the first offset depends on the control and its offset memory, so read one known offset back before a macro writes to any.

Colours form by oxidation; oxygen and water vapour in the furnace gas (air or a leak) colour the surface, a clean inert or vacuum atmosphere does not.
Charts differ by alloy: stainless steels colour at higher temperatures than plain carbon steel, and higher chromium slows the tint.
A rougher or dirty surface oxidises faster and shows deeper colours; clean, bright metal is needed to read a colour at all.

terms.own: Heating steel to a set temperature, holding it and cooling it very slowly (often in the furnace) so it is as soft and machinable as it gets. Tool steels are supplied 'soft annealed'.
A long soak just below or around the lower critical temperature that turns the carbides into small balls; the softest condition for cold forming and machining high-carbon steels.
Heating above the hardening range and cooling in still air. Refines the grain and evens out the structure after forging or rolling; harder than annealed, softer than hardened.

Heating well below the hardening range (for hardened steel, below the last tempering temperature) and cooling slowly, to release stresses from rough machining, welding or straightening without changing hardness much. Tool makers advise it between roughing and finishing.

Heating the steel into its hardening range (austenitising), soaking it until it is heated through, then cooling it fast enough (the quench) to form hard martensite. The quench medium (water, oil, polymer, air, gas) is set by the grade.

Water is the most severe quench, then polymer solutions and oil; air-hardening steels (A2, D2, H13, S7) harden in still or forced air or gas, which distorts less. A martempering (hot bath) quench stops just above the martensite start temperature to even out the part before it cools.

Reheating hardened steel to a temperature below the hardening range, holding it and cooling it. It trades some hardness for toughness and must follow the quench at once (tool makers say when the part reaches about 50-70 °C). Tool steels are usually tempered twice or more.
Quenching into a hot salt bath or fluidised bed held just above the martensite start, equalising, then cooling in air. Less distortion and cracking than a direct quench.
Adding carbon to the surface of a low-carbon steel at high temperature, then hardening, so a hard skin sits on a tough core. Used for gears, pins and wear parts made of grades such as 8620.

Diffusing nitrogen into the surface at a relatively low temperature (around 500 °C) for many hours. No quench, so very little distortion; gives a thin, very hard case on nitriding steels, 4140, 4340, H13 and similar.

Heating only the surface quickly (with an induction coil or a flame) and quenching it, leaving the core as it was. Needs a steel with enough carbon (medium-carbon and alloy steels such as 1045, 4140, 4340), usually followed by a low temper.

For precipitation-hardening stainless steels such as 17-4PH: the bar is supplied solution treated (condition A); a single ageing at a lower temperature then raises strength. The condition name is the ageing temperature in °F (H900 = 900 °F). Ageing shrinks the part slightly.

general.text: Plastics conduct heat poorly and expand up to about ten times as much as metals: keep heat out of the part with sharp, positive tools and enough feed to cut chips rather than rub.
Coolant is mostly not needed: air blast or a water-based fluid. Mineral-oil fluids can stress-crack amorphous plastics (PC, PMMA, PEI, PSU, ABS).
For tight tolerances, rough, let the part rest (MCAM: 24 hours) or anneal it, then finish. Diameters tend to grow after machining, so aim low in the tolerance (MCAM).
Measure at room temperature: a part measured warm from the machine is oversize by its expansion.
Drilling generates the most heat: peck, clear chips, and use a lower speed than turning (MCAM: 25-100 m/min, 90-120° point).
Test on scrap first; grades and fillers change the right numbers.

families.text: A thermoplastic softens and melts when it is heated and sets again when it cools, so it can be melted and shaped again. Named as thermoplastics: polyethylene, polypropylene, polycarbonate, PVC, acrylic, nylon, PTFE and acetal.
A thermoset (epoxy, phenolic, polyurethane, silicone) forms cross-links between its chains when it cures. After that it stays solid when heated and cannot be melted or shaped again.
Thermosets stand heat better; thermoplastics soften as they warm but are tougher and take a knock better.
The sources differ. TWI: thermoplastics are typically more expensive than thermosets. Xometry: most thermoplastics are priced lower than thermosets.
A semi-crystalline plastic has a sharp melting point. An amorphous plastic has none: it softens little by little over a range of temperature.
Amorphous plastics are often transparent or translucent; semi-crystalline plastics are typically opaque.

Semi-crystalline plastics resist chemicals better. Amorphous plastics have limited chemical resistance and are the ones that crack under stress, which is why the coolant matters for them (see General practice).
Semi-crystalline plastics wear better and slide with less friction: the usual choice for wear and bearing parts. Amorphous plastics wear poorly.
Amorphous plastics shrink little and hold their size well. Semi-crystalline plastics shrink more, and not evenly in every direction; Ensinger notes high shrinkage after machining for them.
Semi-crystalline plastics are the stiffer of the two.
Amorphous plastics take impact better than semi-crystalline plastics of a similar grade.
Semi-crystalline plastics have good fatigue resistance; amorphous plastics tire sooner.
Amorphous plastics bond well with adhesives; semi-crystalline plastics are difficult to bond.

The sources differ. Polymershapes: semi-crystalline plastics are generally better in the heat. Xometry: amorphous plastics generally have the higher temperature resistance, to be confirmed for each material. Go by the maximum service temperature of the plastic itself.

tests.text: Touch the metal lightly to a grinding wheel and compare the stream with known samples on the same wheel: more carbon gives more, smaller bursts (sparklers). Wear eye protection and keep clear of others.
Iron-based (ferrous) metals are normally attracted by a magnet and nonferrous metals are not; some stainless steels are not magnetic, so the test is not fully reliable.

Ferritic and martensitic stainless (400 series) are attracted by a magnet, annealed austenitic stainless (300 series) is not, and cold-worked 300 series can be slightly magnetic: a magnet alone never proves a grade.

Cut a small chip with a sharp cold chisel and compare with known samples: the size and edges of the chip, its grain, and how easily it cuts all help to tell metals apart (the Navy manual tabulates them).
A file bites easily into soft (annealed) steel, harder into tool steel, and skates over hardened steel; it gives a rough idea of hardness only. Use a proper hardness tester for numbers.
Colour, surface (mill scale, cast skin, machined), and weight for size separate aluminium, titanium, copper alloys and steel quickly.
For a grade that matters, trust the mill certificate, a positive material identification (XRF or OES) analysis, or a lab: the tests above only sort metals into families.

Metric types A, B, R: 60 deg (DIN 333 title '60 deg centre drills; types R, A and B'; Linear Tools, ZPS). Type B adds a 120 deg protecting chamfer. Pilot point: 118 deg on the US inch tools (Michigan, KEO listings), 120 deg on Linear Tools' tools.

WIKI_SHEET.title: Sheet metal: standard sheet metal gauges
WIKI_SHEET.note: Columns: US standard for sheet and plate iron and steel (cited to Machinery's Handbook and 15 U.S.C. 206), Manufacturers' Standard Gauge for sheet steel, galvanized steel, stainless steel, steel tube wall thickness, aluminium, zinc. Zinc is not entered. Rows 9, 13, 14, 15, 17, 21, 24, 26 and 27 were read a second time cell by cell.

ETB_GAUGE.title: Gauge and weight chart: sheet steel, galvanized steel, stainless steel, aluminum, strip and tubing
ETB_GAUGE.note: US Standard Gauge 44 to 7/0; sheet steel 38 to 3; galvanized 30 to 8 (three places); stainless 38 to 6/0; aluminum 38 to 6/0; strip and tubing 36 to 5/0. Weights per square foot are not entered. A sheet metal supplier's page (riversidesheetmetal.net) prints the same chart and is not counted as a separate publisher.

WIKI_SWG.title: Standard wire gauge
WIKI_SWG.note: SWG 7/0 to 50; defined by BS 3737:1964, since withdrawn; fixed by Order in Council in 1883.

ETB_SWG.title: SWG: Standard Wire Gauge
ETB_SWG.note: SWG 7/0 to 50 in inches and mm; BS 3737:1964, withdrawn. Its mm figure for 1/0 (8.236) does not match its own 0.324 in (8.230 mm); the inch values are entered.

notes.sheet: A gauge number is not one thickness: it depends on the metal. In these tables uncoated steel sheet is the Manufacturers' Standard Gauge, galvanized sheet is listed thicker than uncoated steel of the same number, the stainless steel column is the same as the older US Standard gauge, and the aluminium column is the Brown & Sharpe (American wire) gauge. Order sheet by its thickness and give the gauge only as a name. The two publishers print stainless No. 9 as 0.1563 and 0.1562 in: it is 5/32 in (0.15625) rounded up by one and cut off by the other. For aluminium No. 14 and No. 26 one prints the Brown & Sharpe sizes (0.0641, 0.0159 in) and the other 0.063 and 0.017 in; both are shown. Zinc and copper sheet gauges are not included.
notes.wire: Three different wire gauges share the same numbers. The American wire gauge (AWG, Brown & Sharpe), used mainly in North America for electrical and other nonferrous wire, is worked out here from its rule: 0.005 in x 92^((36 - n) / 39), with No. 36 = 0.005 in and No. 4/0 = 0.46 in. The British Standard Wire Gauge (SWG, BS 3737:1964, withdrawn) is a table. The third column is the series both publishers print for the wall thickness of steel tube and for strip; from No. 7 to 17 it has the same values as the Birmingham gauge, also called the Stubs iron wire gauge. Sizes larger than 0 are written 2/0 (00), 3/0 (000) and so on.

MUTUAL.title: Bolt grade markings and strength chart
MUTUAL.note: Distributor. SAE J429 grades 2/5/8 (Grade 2 printed as ranges, both size bands in one cell, so not recorded per band), ISO 898-1 classes without a size split (8.8 printed once: 800 / 640 / proof 600, recorded under d <= 16). No hardness, no A574.

BOSSARD.title: Technical sheet F-013: marking and mechanical properties of hex head fasteners UNC/UNF according to SAE J429; marking according to ISO 898-1 (revision April 2009)
BOSSARD.note: Fastener maker and distributor. SAE J429 grades 1, 2, 5, 5.2, 8 with size ranges; proof, yield and tensile in psi and MPa. Grade 1 has no grade mark. Parts with reduced loadability are marked with a leading 0 (04.6, 010.9).

WESTFIELD.title: Strength specifications of metric threaded fasteners
WESTFIELD.note: Distributor. Classes 4.6, 4.8, 5.8, 8.8 (16 mm and under / 17-72 mm), 9.8, 10.9, 12.9: proof strength, yield min, tensile min (MPa). Prints the 8.8 proof strengths as 660 (16 mm and under) and 580 (over 16), not in the order Optimas prints.

OPTIMAS.title: Mechanical and physical properties of steel fasteners (EN ISO 898-1)
OPTIMAS.note: Fastener distributor. ISO 898-1 property table: Sp, ReL / Rp0.2 / Rpf, Rm, HV, HB, HR. The 8.8 columns are not labelled on the page; the split is read as d <= 16 / d > 16 from the value order.

MSC.title: Socket head cap screws (socket products handbook: inch 1960 series and metric, pp. 1-16)
MSC.note: Distributor PDF, maker not named. Inch: ASME B18.3 and ASTM A574 (tensile 180,000 psi #2 to 1/2, 170,000 psi over 1/2; yield 162,000 / 153,000; HRC 39 / 37 min). Metric: ASME B18.3.1M and ASTM A574M head and key sizes and minimum tensile loads; drill and counterbore tables (inch p. 5, metric p. 12). The inch head columns came out garbled, so only the hex key column is used. Metric M3 row prints body diameter 2.50 (misprint).

AFT.title: Socket cap screws: dimensions and mechanical properties (ASME B18.3-2003)
AFT.note: Distributor. Inch socket head cap screws #0 to 1 1/2: head diameter and height max/min, hex socket. Alloy steel hardness HRC 39 min (0 to 1/2), HRC 37 min (5/8 and larger).

AMFAST.title: Socket products: socket head cap screws
AMFAST.note: Distributor. Inch socket head cap screws #0 to 1 1/2: head diameter max, head height max, hex socket size. No standard named.

MISUMI.title: Metric socket head cap screw dimensions (blog); counterboring and bolt holes for hexagon socket head cap screws (technical data p. 2847, from JIS B 1176); machine keys and key grooves (technical data, from JIS B 1301:1996)
MISUMI.note: Maker and distributor. Head table follows "ISO specifications" (M1.6 to M48). Counterbore table: hole d', counterbore D', depth H' and H'' for M3 to M30. Key table: the PDF text extraction mixed the parallel-key and taper-key hub depths; the values used are the set that matches JIS B 1301 parallel keys (8 x 7: t2 = 3.3). Non-preferred sizes in brackets are left out.

NBK.title: Diameter of clearance holes and counterbores for bolts and screws (excerpt from JIS B 1001:1985, refers to ISO 273)
NBK.note: Maker. Grades 1, 2, 3 (= ISO 273 fine, medium, coarse) and grade 4 (cast holes, not in ISO 273, in brackets, not recorded). Its counterbore D' is a spot face for hex bolts and is not used.

FRACTORY.title: Metric clearance hole sizes
FRACTORY.note: Manufacturing service. Close / normal / loose fit, M1 to M150, no standard named. Prints M3 normal 3.35 and M6 normal 6.5; prints M30 twice (normal 32 and 33).

OPTIMAS_TAP.title: Tapping sizes: ISO metric coarse with close, medium and free fit clearance holes
OPTIMAS_TAP.note: Close / medium / free fit; no standard named.

TRF.title: Tapping sizes and clearance holes
TRF.note: Fastener maker. One metric clearance column (recorded as medium; it matches the NBK grade 2 values); Unified close and free fit as drill names. Stated as recommendations.

WIKI_AF.title: Width across flats
WIKI_AF.note: Table of ISO widths across flats M2 to M42 (credits ISO 262:1998). Text: ISO 272 (1982) changed M10, M12, M14 and M22 from 17, 19, 22 and 32 mm.

ACCU.title: Across flats bolt size and spanner size chart
ACCU.note: Distributor. Metric: separate ISO rows for M10, M12, M14 and M22 (other rows recorded as both ISO and DIN) and a JIS M8 row (12 mm). Inch rows are hex nut sizes (7/16 -> 11/16, 9/16 -> 7/8), not hex cap screw heads; machine-screw rows not recorded (#6 is printed 5/16 with decimal 0.2500).

SLS.title: Spanner selection chart (hex head bolt)
SLS.note: Distributor. Metric DIN and ISO columns M1.6 to M160; inch ASME and BS columns 1/4 to 3 in.

FASTENIT.title: DIN 6885-1 standard dimensions for parallel keys (edition 08/1968, shown as withdrawn on the page)
FASTENIT.note: Fastener standards portal. b x h, shaft range, t1, t2; lengths from its form B weight tables.

AIMS.title: What is a key and keyway? (keyway guide: ANSI B17.1-1967 (R2013), DIN 6885-1 / ISO 773, Woodruff)
AIMS.note: Distributor. Metric table to 170-200 mm. Inch table with square and rectangular keys and shaft keyseat depth (half the key height). Woodruff list without keyseat depths (not used).

EE_KEY.title: Shaft diameter vs key sizes (design per ANSI B17.1)
EE_KEY.note: Engineering reference site. Square and rectangular key width and height, keyseat depth H/2, shafts 5/16 to 11 in.

AMES_KEY.title: Key size versus shaft diameter per ANSI B17.1-1967 (R1998)
AMES_KEY.note: Engineering calculator site. Only the shaft diameter ranges are in the page text (key sizes are in an image), so it confirms the ranges only.

EE_TSLOT.title: Dimension table for T-slots, bolts and nuts (ANSI/ASME B5.1M-1985), mm columns
EE_TSLOT.note: Engineering reference site. Throat width (= slot width a), headspace width and depth min-max in inch and mm; it prints the depth of the throat, not the total slot depth, so h is not taken from it.

ITEH_299.title: ISO 299:1987 Machine tool tables - T-slots and corresponding bolts (preview)
ITEH_299.note: Standards distributor preview. The OCR text is partly garbled; only the clearly readable b, c and h min-max, the bolt thread and the pitches are taken. Slot width tolerance H12 (fixing slots), H8 (reference slots).

GTWEED.title: AS568 O-ring size chart ("O-Ring Seals")
GTWEED.note: Seal maker. Dash numbers -005 to -475 and -901 to -914: ID and CS with tolerances, inch. Prints -391 ID 21.995 where the -471 row of the same step prints 21.955.

EFUNDA.title: O-ring AS568 sizes
EFUNDA.note: Engineering reference site. Detailed rows only for -001 to -050 and -102 to -114.

ORINGSINC.title: AS568A size chart (PDF)
ORINGSINC.note: Distributor. The text extraction lost the alignment of most rows; only rows printed clearly with their dash number are used (about every tenth size).

BOSSARD_F044.title: Technical sheet TF.049 (F-en-2023.05): friction coefficient classes A to E for muG and muK, according to VDI 2230 (2015), room temperature
BOSSARD_F044.note: Fastener maker. The aim is class B for a high preload with little scatter. Descriptions are summarised in BenchMate's words.

HAMEEDI.title: Experimental determination of torque and friction coefficients in the torque-preload relationships of bolted connections, ÉPKO 2025
HAMEEDI.note: Conference paper. Eq. (3): T = Fv [0.16 p + 0.58 mu_t dm + 0.5 mu_h dh], attributed to Motosh and VDI 2230. Measured mean friction 0.13 to 0.44 on M16-M24 structural bolts (dry highest, oiled lowest).

FVA.title: FVA-Workbench 9 documentation: bolt connection (VDI 2230-1:2015, eq. 229-231 and 259)
FVA.note: Software maker. MA = FMzul (0.16 P + 0.58 d2 muGmin + DKm/2 muKmin); FMzul = A0 nu Rp0.2min / sqrt(1 + 3 [3/2 d2/d0 (P/(pi d2) + 1.155 muGmin)]^2), nu normally 0.9.

BOSSARD_VDI.title: Approximate values for metric coarse threads, VDI 2230 (assumptions page)
BOSSARD_VDI.note: Tables based on VDI 2230 (2015), 90 % utilisation of ReL / Rp0.2, clearance holes ISO 273 medium; values are maximums without a safety factor and higher than the 1986 edition.

MAREK.publisher: marek.eu (catalogue technical pages, publisher not named)
MAREK.title: Technical information: screws and nuts, pp. 1287-1288 (VDI 2230 clamping forces and tightening torques)
MAREK.note: Torques computed with muG = muK. Used only as a worked-example check of the torque formula in core/src/fasteners.rs.

GLOBAL_ORING.title: O-ring groove design
GLOBAL_ORING.note: Seal distributor. All compression values between 5 % and 30 % squeeze; static seals typically 15-30 %; dynamic less; design for roughly 60-85 % groove fill, never 100 %; installed stretch max 5 %; rod gland OD compression max 2 %; face seal OD up to 3 % over (internal pressure) or ID up to 5 % under (external pressure).

APPLE.title: Seal design guide: O-ring installation
APPLE.note: Seal maker. Squeeze about 10-40 % static, no more than 30 % dynamic; O-ring volume not over 90 % of the minimum gland void; at least 75 % of the cross-section inside the groove; stretch not over 5 % in the application, not over 100 % while installing.

BOLTS_4017.title: ISO 4017, hexagon head screw (dimension table)
BOLTS_4017.note: Open library of standard parts for CAD (J. Reinhardt and contributors). Head height k and width across flats s for M1.6 to M64; M3 to M36 recorded. Its width across corners at M10 and M12 belongs to the old 17 and 19 mm heads and is not recorded.

FEU_4014.title: ISO 4014, hexagon head bolts with shank (table headed DIN 931, ISO 4014)
FEU_4014.note: Fastener trade directory. Head height K (one value per size) recorded. FASTENIT_4032.title: DIN EN ISO 4032, hexagon nuts, style 1 (edition 04-2013)
FASTENIT_4032.note: Fastener trade directory. Nut height m max and min and width across flats (nominal). Its M6 (5 / 4.7) and M24 (19 / 17.7) heights differ from the two other publishers; M24 is lower than its own M22 row (19.4 / 18.1). Recorded as printed.

WERMAC_NUT.title: Metric nut dimensions chart, across flats and heights (ISO 4032)
WERMAC_NUT.note: Piping reference site. Width across flats max and min and nut height max and min.

OMDL_4032.title: ISO 4032 hexagon nut data table, omdl v1.0 documentation
OMDL_4032.note: Documentation of an open design library (R. A. Sutton). Width across flats max and min, width across corners min, thickness max and min.

BOLTS_7089.note: One hole diameter d1, one outside diameter d2 and one thickness s per size. Its M10 hole is printed as 10.0, where fasteners.eu prints 10.5; recorded as printed.

EUGENE_NUT.note: Distributor. Width across flats and thickness as fractions for coarse-thread sizes; names ASME B18.2.2 for its inch values.
